role_in_parent: Covers one of the residue classes that the last failed attempt explicitly omitted; this repairs the missing-coverage defect.
statement_nl: Let p be a prime number with p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8). For each k in {1,2,...,p-1}, let I(k) be the unique integer in {1,2,...,p-1} such that k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p), and define S = { k in {1,2,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then |S| >= floor(p/4).

domain_restrictions: p is an integer and prime
k ranges over integers 1,2,...,p-1 when defining I(k); in S, k ranges over 1,2,...,p-2 so that k+1 ≤ p-1
I(k) is required to be an integer representative in {1,...,p-1} (i.e. nonzero residue class mod p)
Order comparison I(k+1) < I(k) uses the usual ordering of integers
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every prime p with p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8), define I: {1,...,p-1} → {1,...,p-1} by the rule k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p) (unique representative). Let S = { k ∈ {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then the cardinality of S satisfies |S| ≥ ⌊p/4⌋.
quantifier_order: for all p (p is an integer prime, with p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8))
define I as: for all k in {1,...,p-1}, I(k) is the unique element of {1,...,p-1} with k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p)
define S = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }

variables.name: p
variables.role: parameter; prime modulus subject to constraints p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8)

variables.name: k
variables.role: index used to define inverses I(k); later restricted to {1,...,p-2} when forming S

variables.name: I
variables.role: multiplicative inverse modulo p: for each k in {1,..,p-1}, I(k) is the unique r in {1,..,p-1} with k * r ≡ 1 (mod p)

variables.name: S
variables.role: S = { k in {1,..,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) } whose cardinality is compared to floor(p/4)

variables.name: floor(p/4)
variables.role: numeric lower bound for |S| depending on p

witness_dependencies: I(k) depends on both p and k; for each fixed p and k there is a unique witness I(k) in {1,..,p-1} solving k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p)
S depends on p through the function I(·) (so membership of k in S depends on p and on values I(k) and I(k+1))
